claim: Sensory deprivation during development induces lifelong changes to central nervous system function that are associated with perceptual impairments.
source: Sensory deprivation during development induces lifelong changes to central nervous system function that are associated with perceptual impairments.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The relationship between neural and behavioral deficits following sensory deprivation is uncertain due to a lack of simultaneous measurements during task performance.
source: However, the relationship between neural and behavioral deficits is uncertain due to a lack of simultaneous measurements during task performance.
evidence: This statement is supported by the extensive citation list in the Introduction discussing the dramatic differences in sensory-evoked responses during task engagement versus disengagement.

claim: Developmental HL diminished behavioral performance on an auditory task detecting rapid fluctuations in amplitude.
source: We found that developmental HL diminished behavioral performance, but did not alter brainstem temporal processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the psychometric data presented in Figure 1, showing significantly worse thresholds for HL animals at 128, 256, and 512 Hz.

claim: Developmental HL did not alter brainstem temporal processing.
source: We found that developmental HL diminished behavioral performance, but did not alter brainstem temporal processing.
evidence: This is supported by the EFR data in Figure 4G showing no significant difference between Ctl and HL groups in brainstem TMTFs.

claim: Perceptual deficits following developmental HL were associated with a degraded cortical population code.
source: However, the simultaneous assessment of neural and behavioral processing revealed that perceptual deficits were associated with a degraded cortical population code that could be explained by greater trial-to-trial response variability.
evidence: This is supported by the population decoder analysis in Figure 7D showing inferior performance for HL units at lower AM depths.

claim: Greater trial-to-trial response variability explains the degraded cortical population code in HL animals.
source: However, the simultaneous assessment of neural and behavioral processing revealed that perceptual deficits were associated with a degraded cortical population code that could be explained by greater trial-to-trial response variability.
evidence: This is supported by the CV data in Figure 6A showing significantly greater trial-to-trial variability among HL units.

claim: The perceptual limitations that attend early hearing loss are best explained by an encoding deficit in auditory cortex.
source: Our findings suggest that the perceptual limitations that attend early hearing loss are best explained by an encoding deficit in auditory cortex.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined findings that brainstem processing was not impaired but cortical population encoding was degraded in HL animals.

claim: Many forms of developmental deprivation induce lifelong behavioral deficits associated with degraded CNS function.
source: Many forms of developmental deprivation, including the loss of hearing or vision, induce lifelong behavioral deficits that are associated with degraded central nervous system (CNS) function (Kiorpes, 2006; Petersen, 2007; Kalinichev and Francis, 2010; Sanes and Woolley, 2011; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The precise relationship between perception and sensory coding following sensory deprivation is uncertain because measurements are generally obtained from separate groups of animals.
source: However, the precise relationship between perception and sensory coding following sensory deprivation is uncertain because measurements are generally obtained from separate groups of animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research methodology.

claim: Sensory-evoked responses differ dramatically during task engagement versus disengagement.
source: This uncertainty can be attributed, in part, to the dramatic differences of sensory-evoked responses elicited during task engagement versus disengagement (Hubel et al., 1959; Burton et al., 1997; Spitzer et al., 1988; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999a; 1999b; Treue and Maunsell, 1999; Reynolds et al., 2000; Steinmetz et al., 2000; Fritz et al., 2003; 2005; Chapman and Meftah, 2005; Elhilali et al., 2007; Cohen and Newsome, 2008; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Otazu et al., 2009; Lee and Middlebrooks, 2011; David et al., 2012; Niwa et al., 2015; Buran et al., 2014b; Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015; Slee and David, 2015; von Trapp et al., 2016; Carcea et al., 2017; Caras and Sanes, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by extensive citations to previous research.

claim: Permanent HL induced during early development can impair neural encoding mechanisms throughout the auditory pathway.
source: Since permanent HL induced during early development can impair neural encoding mechanisms throughout the auditory pathway, many candidate mechanisms have been suggested (Knudsen et al., 1982; 1984a; 1984b; Mogdans and Knudsen, 1993; Mogdans and Knudsen, 1994; Raggio and Schreiner, 1999; Snyder et al., 2000; DeBello et al., 2001; Moore et al., 1999; Yu et al., 2005; Takahashi et al., 2006; Fallon et al., 2008; Razak et al., 2008; Popescu and Polley, 2010; Rosen et al., 2012; Polley et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Children deprived of normal auditory input early in life display permanent CNS changes and diminished perceptual sensitivity to spectral and temporal features of natural sounds.
source: When children are deprived of normal auditory input early in life, they display permanent CNS changes and diminished perceptual sensitivity to the spectral and temporal features that comprise natural sounds (Ponton and Eggermont, 2001; Sharma et al., 2007; Gilley et al., 2008; Park et al., 2015; Landsberger et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Temporal fluctuations in sound level support speech comprehension and perceptions of rhythm, prosody, musical attack, and pitch.
source: One set of features, temporal fluctuations in sound level, support speech comprehension, and perceptions of rhythm, prosody, musical attack, and pitch (Burns and Viemeister, 1976; Singh and Theunissen, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Perceptual sensitivity to amplitude modulation cues displays a relatively prolonged period of developmental maturation, with detection improving into adolescence.
source: Despite the importance of these amplitude modulation (AM) cues for aural communication, perceptual sensitivity to these signals displays a relatively prolonged period of developmental maturation, with detection improving into adolescence (Hall and Grose, 1994; Sarro and Sanes, 2010; Banai et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: Prolonged maturation of temporal processing suggests it could be vulnerable to environmental experience, including HL.
source: This prolonged maturation suggests that temporal processing could be vulnerable to environmental experience, including HL.
evidence: This is an inference based on the prolonged developmental maturation period.

claim: Developmental HL impairs AM sensitivity and discriminability, particularly for fast (>100 Hz) modulation rates.
source: In fact, there is clinical and experimental evidence demonstrating that developmental HL impairs AM sensitivity and discriminability, particularly for fast (>100 Hz) modulation rates (Bacon and Viemeister, 1985; Grant et al., 1998; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical and experimental studies.

claim: Developmental HL can occur in children with otitis media.
source: Recent studies have shown that developmental HL, which can occur in children with otitis media (Gravel and Wallace, 2000; Whitton and Polley, 2011), leads to long-lasting cellular deficits in auditory cortex (ACx) (Xu et al., 2007; Takesian et al., 2012; Mowery et al., 2015; 2016; 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Developmental HL leads to long-lasting cellular deficits in auditory cortex.
source: Recent studies have shown that developmental HL, which can occur in children with otitis media (Gravel and Wallace, 2000; Whitton and Polley, 2011), leads to long-lasting cellular deficits in auditory cortex (ACx) (Xu et al., 2007; Takesian et al., 2012; Mowery et al., 2015; 2016; 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A HL-induced ACx encoding deficit could explain degraded behavioral performance.
source: Therefore, it is plausible that a HL-induced ACx encoding deficit could explain, in part, degraded behavioral performance (Rosen et al., 2012; Buran et al., 2014a; Caras and Sanes, 2015; von Trapp et al., 2017; Ihlefeld et al., 2016; Green et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous research.

claim: AM detection thresholds displayed a significant interaction between hearing status and AM rate.
source: AM thresholds displayed a significant interaction between hearing status and AM rate (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(3,48) = 30.3, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the psychometric data analysis.

claim: Thresholds from HL animals were similar to Ctl animals at 64 Hz AM rate.
source: Thresholds from HL animals were similar to Ctl animals at the slowest AM rate tested, 64 Hz (p>0.05, t = 2.07), but were markedly worse at 128 Hz (p<0.05, t = 2.75) and 256 Hz (p<0.0001, t = 9.41), and displayed the greatest deficit at 512 Hz (p<0.0001, t = 12.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of psychometric data.

claim: Thresholds from HL animals were markedly worse than Ctl animals at 128 Hz AM rate.
source: Thresholds from HL animals were similar to Ctl animals at the slowest AM rate tested, 64 Hz (p>0.05, t = 2.07), but were markedly worse at 128 Hz (p<0.05, t = 2.75) and 256 Hz (p<0.0001, t = 9.41), and displayed the greatest deficit at 512 Hz (p<0.0001, t = 12.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of psychometric data.

claim: Thresholds from HL animals were markedly worse than Ctl animals at 256 Hz AM rate.
source: Thresholds from HL animals were similar to Ctl animals at the slowest AM rate tested, 64 Hz (p>0.05, t = 2.07), but were markedly worse at 128 Hz (p<0.05, t = 2.75) and 256 Hz (p<0.0001, t = 9.41), and displayed the greatest deficit at 512 Hz (p<0.0001, t = 12.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of psychometric data.

claim: HL animals displayed the greatest deficit at 512 Hz AM rate.
source: Thresholds from HL animals were similar to Ctl animals at the slowest AM rate tested, 64 Hz (p>0.05, t = 2.07), but were markedly worse at 128 Hz (p<0.05, t = 2.75) and 256 Hz (p<0.0001, t = 9.41), and displayed the greatest deficit at 512 Hz (p<0.0001, t = 12.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of psychometric data.

claim: Gain values were similar between Ctl and HL groups.
source: Although gain values were similar between Ctl and HL groups (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; p>0.05, Z = 1.73), HL animals displayed steeper slopes (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; p<0.0005, Z = 3.51).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the TMTF analysis.

claim: HL animals displayed steeper TMTF slopes than Ctl animals.
source: Although gain values were similar between Ctl and HL groups (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; p>0.05, Z = 1.73), HL animals displayed steeper slopes (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; p<0.0005, Z = 3.51).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the TMTF analysis.

claim: Both Ctl and HL animals are equally sensitive to slow AM (64 Hz).
source: This suggests that while both Ctl and HL animals are equally sensitive to slow AM (64 Hz), HL animals possessed poorer temporal resolution across very fast rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TMTF gain and slope data.

claim: HL animals possessed poorer temporal resolution across very fast AM rates.
source: This suggests that while both Ctl and HL animals are equally sensitive to slow AM (64 Hz), HL animals possessed poorer temporal resolution across very fast rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TMTF gain and slope data.

claim: No significant differences were observed for maximum d' between Ctl and HL animals.
source: Specifically, no significant differences were observed for maximum d' (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Ctl median: 2.24 ± 0.23; HL median: 2.22 ± 0.25; p>0.05, Z = 1.91), false alarm rate (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Ctl median: 0.27 ± 0.04; HL median: 0.27 ± 0.06; p>0.05, Z = 1.31), or lapse rate (Ctl median: 3.08 ± 2.99%; HL median: 2.78 ± 3.48%; two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum; p>0.05, Z = 0.38).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral performance analysis.

claim: No significant differences were observed for false alarm rate between Ctl and HL animals.
source: Specifically, no significant differences were observed for maximum d' (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Ctl median: 2.24 ± 0.23; HL median: 2.22 ± 0.25; p>0.05, Z = 1.91), false alarm rate (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Ctl median: 0.27 ± 0.04; HL median: 0.27 ± 0.06; p>0.05, Z = 1.31), or lapse rate (Ctl median: 3.08 ± 2.99%; HL median: 2.78 ± 3.48%; two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum; p>0.05, Z = 0.38).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral performance analysis.

claim: No significant differences were observed for lapse rate between Ctl and HL animals.
source: Specifically, no significant differences were observed for maximum d' (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Ctl median: 2.24 ± 0.23; HL median: 2.22 ± 0.25; p>0.05, Z = 1.91), false alarm rate (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; Ctl median: 0.27 ± 0.04; HL median: 0.27 ± 0.06; p>0.05, Z = 1.31), or lapse rate (Ctl median: 3.08 ± 2.99%; HL median: 2.78 ± 3.48%; two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum; p>0.05, Z = 0.38).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral performance analysis.

claim: No main effect of group (Ctl versus HL) was observed for trials when animals approached the water spout.
source: No main effect of group (Ctl versus HL) was observed for trials when animals approached the water spout (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,5266) = 3.97, p>0.05) or for trials when animals repoked (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,2514) = 0.18, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the response latency analysis.

claim: No main effect of group (Ctl versus HL) was observed for trials when animals repoked.
source: No main effect of group (Ctl versus HL) was observed for trials when animals approached the water spout (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,5266) = 3.97, p>0.05) or for trials when animals repoked (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,2514) = 0.18, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the response latency analysis.

claim: There were no systematic behavioral differences in motor behavior between Ctl versus HL animals during psychometric testing.
source: This suggests that there were no systematic behavioral differences in motor behavior between Ctl versus HL animals during psychometric testing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the response latency data.

claim: Poorer AM detection thresholds observed in the HL group was not due to a diminished ability to perform the task.
source: Together, these analyses suggest that poorer AM detection thresholds observed in the HL group (Figure 1B) was not due to a diminished ability to perform the task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined behavioral performance metrics.

claim: Animals were not responding to an average level cue during AM detection.
source: In contrast, each individual animal displayed robust AM detection with d' values > 2, and performance did not vary with average sound level (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2 showing no correlation between d' and sound level.

claim: Linear fit slopes of d' versus sound level did not significantly vary from 0 across four AM rates tested.
source: Across the four AM rates tested, linear fit slopes did not significantly vary from 0 (range: 0.00–0.006; one-sample t-test; p>0.05, t = 0.17–1.78), indicating that the sensory decision was not based on stimulus level.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sound level roving experiment.

claim: The sensory decision was not based on stimulus level.
source: Across the four AM rates tested, linear fit slopes did not significantly vary from 0 (range: 0.00–0.006; one-sample t-test; p>0.05, t = 0.17–1.78), indicating that the sensory decision was not based on stimulus level.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sound level roving data.

claim: ABR thresholds to clicks were ~39 dB higher in HL versus Ctl animals.
source: ABR thresholds to clicks, a general measure of brainstem function, were ~39 dB higher in HL versus Ctl animals (Figure 3A; two-sample t-test; p<10−4, t = −15.48).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ABR threshold measurements.

claim: No significant correlations were observed between ABR click thresholds and AM detection performance for either the HL or Ctl group.
source: No significant correlations were observed for either the HL (Pearson's r = 0.27–0.52, p>0.05) or Ctl group (Pearson's r = 0.35–68, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis between ABR and behavior.

claim: ABR amplitudes grew significantly larger as sensation level increased.
source: In addition, as illustrated in Figure 3C (top), ABR amplitudes grew significantly larger as sensation level increased (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 127.6, p<0.0001), but there was no main effect of hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 0.18, p>0.05), nor was there an interaction between sensation level and hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(6,90) = 1.12, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ABR amplitude analysis.

claim: There was no main effect of hearing status on ABR amplitudes.
source: In addition, as illustrated in Figure 3C (top), ABR amplitudes grew significantly larger as sensation level increased (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 127.6, p<0.0001), but there was no main effect of hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 0.18, p>0.05), nor was there an interaction between sensation level and hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(6,90) = 1.12, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ABR amplitude analysis.

claim: There was no interaction between sensation level and hearing status for ABR amplitudes.
source: In addition, as illustrated in Figure 3C (top), ABR amplitudes grew significantly larger as sensation level increased (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 127.6, p<0.0001), but there was no main effect of hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 0.18, p>0.05), nor was there an interaction between sensation level and hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(6,90) = 1.12, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ABR amplitude analysis.

claim: ABR peak latencies significantly decreased with increasing sensation level.
source: Furthermore, ABR peak latencies significantly decreased with increasing sensation level (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 537.4, p<0.0001), but there was no main effect of hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 0.74, p>0.05), nor was there an interaction between sensation level and hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(6,90) = 1, p>0.05) (Figure 3C, bottom).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ABR latency analysis.

claim: There was no main effect of hearing status on ABR peak latencies.
source: Furthermore, ABR peak latencies significantly decreased with increasing sensation level (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 537.4, p<0.0001), but there was no main effect of hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 0.74, p>0.05), nor was there an interaction between sensation level and hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(6,90) = 1, p>0.05) (Figure 3C, bottom).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ABR latency analysis.

claim: There was no interaction between sensation level and hearing status for ABR peak latencies.
source: Furthermore, ABR peak latencies significantly decreased with increasing sensation level (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 537.4, p<0.0001), but there was no main effect of hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(1,15) = 0.74, p>0.05), nor was there an interaction between sensation level and hearing status (two-way mixed model ANOVA; F(6,90) = 1, p>0.05) (Figure 3C, bottom).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ABR latency analysis.

claim: Elevated ABR click thresholds did not account for poorer AM sensitivity in the HL group.
source: Thus, elevated ABR click thresholds did not account for poorer AM sensitivity in the HL group, presumably because behavioral testing was performed at the same sensation level.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ABR and behavioral data.

claim: EFR thresholds were not significantly different for Ctl and HL groups.
source: The TMTFs obtained from EFRs were not significantly different for Ctl and HL groups (two-way Mixed Model ANOVA; interaction: F(3,45) = 0.84, p>0.05), suggesting that our recordings do not reveal a HL-related impairment.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the EFR TMTF analysis.

claim: EFR recordings do not reveal a HL-related impairment.
source: The TMTFs obtained from EFRs were not significantly different for Ctl and HL groups (two-way Mixed Model ANOVA; interaction: F(3,45) = 0.84, p>0.05), suggesting that our recordings do not reveal a HL-related impairment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EFR TMTF data.

claim: Ctl animals displayed similar behavior and EFR-based AM thresholds.
source: Ctl animals displayed similar behavior and EFR-based AM thresholds (two-way repeated measures ANOVA; interaction: F(3,42) = 1.81, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of behavior and EFR thresholds.

claim: Behavior and EFR-based AM thresholds were significantly different for the HL group.
source: In contrast, behavior and EFR-based AM thresholds were significantly different for the HL group (two-way repeated measures ANOVA; interaction: F(3,42) = 12.6, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of behavior and EFR thresholds.

claim: Behavioral thresholds were markedly worse than EFR thresholds for 256 Hz in HL animals.
source: Post-hoc analyses indicated behavioral thresholds were markedly worse than EFR thresholds for 256 Hz (two-tailed t-test, Holm-Bonferroni-corrected; t = 4.09, p<0.05) and 512 Hz (two-tailed t-test, Holm-Bonferroni-corrected; t = 8.31, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: Behavioral thresholds were markedly worse than EFR thresholds for 512 Hz in HL animals.
source: Post-hoc analyses indicated behavioral thresholds were markedly worse than EFR thresholds for 256 Hz (two-tailed t-test, Holm-Bonferroni-corrected; t = 4.09, p<0.05) and 512 Hz (two-tailed t-test, Holm-Bonferroni-corrected; t = 8.31, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: EFR measurements do not account for the HL-induced perceptual deficits at fast AM rates.
source: These results suggest that our recorded EFR measurements do not account for the HL-induced perceptual deficits at fast AM rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EFR and behavioral data.

claim: 21% of recorded units were classified as single-units.
source: We recorded from a total of 460 units where 21% were classified as single-units.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the electrophysiology recordings.

claim: Significant phase locking was not observed for ACx units across all AM rates tested, regardless of hearing status.
source: Consistent with a broad literature, significant phase locking was not observed for ACx units across all AM rates tested, regardless of hearing status (median VS = 0.10, interquartile range = 0.07–0.14; median Rayleigh statistic = 3.99, interquartile range = 2.87–5.66).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the vector strength analysis.

claim: Driven and spontaneous FRs were significantly greater among Ctl units.
source: We found that driven and spontaneous FRs were significantly greater among Ctl units (two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; Driven FR: K = 0.12, p=0.005; Spont FR: K = 0.27, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of ACx unit properties.

claim: CV was significantly lower among Ctl units.
source: CV was significantly lower among Ctl units (two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; K = 0.24, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison of ACx unit properties.

claim: Spontaneous activity tended to be fairly high, and occasionally higher than the driven FR suggesting significant inhibition after stimulus onset.
source: Spontaneous activity tended to be fairly high, and occasionally higher than the driven FR suggesting that there was significant inhibition after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spontaneous and driven firing rate data.

claim: Using a bootstrapped statistical test, there was no significant difference in FR between Ctl versus HL units.
source: Using this more conservative approach, we found no significant difference in FR between Ctl versus HL units (confidence interval (CI) = [−3.09 2.99], p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the bootstrapped analysis.

claim: Spont FR remained significantly higher among Ctl units using a bootstrapped statistical test.
source: However, Spont FR remained significantly higher among Ctl units (CI = [1.59 9.04], p<0.05) and CV remained significantly lower among Ctl units (CI = [−0.14–0.04], p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the bootstrapped analysis.

claim: CV remained significantly lower among Ctl units using a bootstrapped statistical test.
source: However, Spont FR remained significantly higher among Ctl units (CI = [1.59 9.04], p<0.05) and CV remained significantly lower among Ctl units (CI = [−0.14–0.04], p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the bootstrapped analysis.

claim: The difference in overall FR might be related to unit sampling.
source: Thus, whereas the difference in overall FR might be related to unit sampling, responses from ACx units in HL-reared animals were significantly less reliable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the bootstrapped analysis results.

claim: Responses from ACx units in HL-reared animals were significantly less reliable.
source: Thus, whereas the difference in overall FR might be related to unit sampling, responses from ACx units in HL-reared animals were significantly less reliable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CV data.

claim: 51.7% of recorded units displayed increases in FR with greater AM depth.
source: Increases in FR with greater AM depth was observed in 51.7% of recorded units (e.g., Figure 6B, left; open circles and triangles), whereas the remaining 48.3% of units displayed a decrease in FR with increasing AM depth (e.g., Figure 6B, left; open squares).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the FR analysis.

claim: 48.3% of recorded units displayed a decrease in FR with increasing AM depth.
source: Increases in FR with greater AM depth was observed in 51.7% of recorded units (e.g., Figure 6B, left; open circles and triangles), whereas the remaining 48.3% of units displayed a decrease in FR with increasing AM depth (e.g., Figure 6B, left; open squares).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the FR analysis.

claim: The distributions of FR-based AM thresholds from Ctl and HL units did not differ from one another.
source: The distributions did not differ from one another (Interaction, F(3,210) = 1.72, p>0.05; Two-way Mixed Model ANOVA), and most unit thresholds were poorer than behavioral thresholds.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the neurometric threshold analysis.

claim: Most unit thresholds were poorer than behavioral thresholds.
source: The distributions did not differ from one another (Interaction, F(3,210) = 1.72, p>0.05; Two-way Mixed Model ANOVA), and most unit thresholds were poorer than behavioral thresholds.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the neurometric threshold analysis.

claim: The K-means metric outperformed the FR, Rcorr, and Van Rossum metrics in correlating with psychometric thresholds.
source: The K-means metric (Pearson's r = 0.46) outperformed the FR (Pearson's r = 0.38), Rcorr (Pearson's r = 0.30), and Van Rossum (Pearson's r = 0.25) metrics, and displayed the strongest correlation with psychometric thresholds.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the classifier analysis.

claim: 38.9% of Ctl units displayed K-means thresholds that were similar to psychometric performance.
source: As illustrated in Figure 6D , a greater percentage of units displayed K-means thresholds that were similar to psychometric performance (Ctl units: 38.9%; HL units: 38.6%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the K-means classifier analysis.

claim: 38.6% of HL units displayed K-means thresholds that were similar to psychometric performance.
source: As illustrated in Figure 6D , a greater percentage of units displayed K-means thresholds that were similar to psychometric performance (Ctl units: 38.9%; HL units: 38.6%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the K-means classifier analysis.

claim: There was no significant interaction between Ctl and HL groups across AM rates for K-means thresholds.
source: However, we did not find a significant interaction between Ctl and HL groups across AM rates (F(3,768) = 0.71, p>0.05; Two-way Mixed Model ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the K-means classifier analysis.

claim: Unit-by-unit analyses of cortical AM encoding do not entirely reflect the HL-induced perceptual deficits.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the unit-by-unit analyses of cortical AM encoding do not entirely reflect the HL-induced perceptual deficits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neurometric and classifier analyses.

claim: Both Ctl and HL groups displayed greater d' with increasing unit counts.
source: Both Ctl and HL groups displayed greater d' with increasing unit counts with the highest d' values seen when all units within each group were utilized.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the population decoder analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Maximum decoder performance was uniformly better among units from both groups tested at the 256 Hz AM rate.
source: Maximum decoder performance was uniformly better among units from both groups tested at the 256 Hz AM rate.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the population decoder analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The superior decoder performance at 256 Hz could be due to a sampling bias.
source: This could be due to a sampling bias since we would initially search for unit responses that were driven by 256 or 512 Hz AM noise during each electrode advancement (see Materials and Methods).
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the 256 Hz decoder performance.

claim: Higher AM depths yielded greater d' values for both groups in the population decoder.
source: Typically, higher AM depths yielded greater d' values for both groups, but decoder performance from HL units was worse than Ctl units at lower AM depths.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the population decoder analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Decoder performance from HL units was worse than Ctl units at lower AM depths.
source: Typically, higher AM depths yielded greater d' values for both groups, but decoder performance from HL units was worse than Ctl units at lower AM depths.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the population decoder analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: For AM rates at which a clear behavioral deficit was observed for HL animals (256 and 512 Hz), HL population decoder performance was inferior at lower depths, near behavioral threshold.
source: For AM rates at which a clear behavioral deficit was observed for HL animals (256 and 512 Hz), HL population decoder performance was inferior at lower depths, near behavioral threshold (256 Hz: ≤ −6 dB rel. 100%; 512 Hz: ≤ −3 dB rel. 100%).
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the population decoder analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Decoder performance was better for monotonically decreasing units across most AM depths at 128 and 256 Hz from both Ctl and HL groups.
source: Decoder performance was better for monotonically decreasing units across most AM depths at 128 and 256 Hz from both Ctl and HL groups.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the monotonicity analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Ctl monotonically decreasing units yielded greater d' values compared to HL monotonically decreasing units across all AM depths.
source: In addition, Ctl monotonically decreasing units yielded greater d' values compared to HL monotonically decreasing units across all AM depths.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the monotonicity analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The HL-related AM detection deficits are reflected in the population activity of ACx units.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the HL-related AM detection deficits (Figure 1) are reflected in the population activity of ACx units.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the population decoder results.

claim: Trial-to-trial variability in FR (CV) was significantly greater among HL units.
source: We reported earlier that trial-to-trial variability in FR (CV; Figure 6A, right) was significantly greater among HL units.
evidence: This refers back to the CV data presented earlier.

claim: Greater trial-to-trial variability among ACx responses of HL units may account for the differences seen in the population decoder outputs between Ctl versus HL units.
source: It is possible that greater trial-to-trial variability among ACx responses of HL units may account for the differences seen in the population decoder outputs between Ctl versus HL units (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the decoder differences.

claim: Population-level variability metric was significantly greater for HL versus Ctl units across all AM rates and depths tested.
source: We found that this variability metric was significantly greater for HL versus Ctl units across all AM rates and depths tested (two-sample Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; p<0.001, z = −2.63 to −16.1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the population-level variability analysis.

claim: CP values did not differ from chance during the 0–400 ms time window, regardless of hearing status group.
source: Regardless of hearing status group, CP values did not differ from chance, either during the 0–400 ms time window (H0: average CP value = 0.50; Ctl: p>0.05, t = −0.03; HL: p>0.05, t = 1.75; one-sample t-test), or the 400–800 ms window (Ctl: p>0.05, t = 0.24; HL: p>0.05, t = 1.52; one-sample t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the choice probability analysis.

claim: CP values did not differ from chance during the 400–800 ms time window, regardless of hearing status group.
source: Regardless of hearing status group, CP values did not differ from chance, either during the 0–400 ms time window (H0: average CP value = 0.50; Ctl: p>0.05, t = −0.03; HL: p>0.05, t = 1.75; one-sample t-test), or the 400–800 ms window (Ctl: p>0.05, t = 0.24; HL: p>0.05, t = 1.52; one-sample t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the choice probability analysis.

claim: Recorded ACx units did not represent the animals' behavioral choice during task performance.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that our recorded ACx units did not represent the animals' behavioral choice during task performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the choice probability results.

claim: No awake-behaving studies have simultaneously assessed neural and perceptual plasticity following early sensory deprivation.
source: While many normative studies have utilized awake-behaving preparations, none have exploited the paradigm to simultaneously assess neural and perceptual plasticity following early sensory deprivation (Knudsen et al., 1982; 1984a; 1984b; Mogdans and Knudsen, 1993; 1994; Raggio and Schreiner, 1999; Snyder et al., 2000; DeBello et al., 2001; Moore et al., 2002; Yu et al., 2005; Takahashi et al., 2006; Fallon et al., 2008; Razak et al., 2008; Popescu and Polley, 2010; Rosen et al., 2012; Polley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study based on a review of the literature.

claim: Depending on the type of deprivation and its age of onset, many subcortical structures can display functional impairments.
source: Furthermore, neural studies suggest that, depending on the type of deprivation and its age of onset, many subcortical structures can display functional impairments (for review, see Sanes and Woolley, 2011; Sanes, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The extent to which neural processing deficits in primary sensory cortex are associated with diminished perceptual performance is uncertain.
source: Therefore, the extent to which neural processing deficits in primary sensory cortex are associated with diminished perceptual performance is uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty in the field that motivates the current study.

claim: Developmental HL impairs behavioral detection of temporal envelope cues that support aural communication and perceptual qualities of rhythm, prosody, periodicity pitch, and musical attack.
source: Here, we report that developmental HL impairs behavioral detection of temporal envelope cues (Figure 1B) that support aural communication and the perceptual qualities of rhythm, prosody, periodicity pitch, and musical attack.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings with reference to the functional significance of AM cues.

claim: The findings are consistent with clinical studies that report poorer AM sensitivity at fast rates (>100 Hz) in profoundly deaf children, congenitally deaf adults, and even late onset HL adults.
source: These findings are consistent with clinical studies that report poorer AM sensitivity at fast rates (>100 Hz) in profoundly deaf children, congenitally deaf adults, and even late onset HL adults (Formby, 1987; Grant et al., 1998; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to previous clinical research.

claim: Basic performance metrics did not differ significantly between groups, pointing to a sensory processing deficit.
source: Since basic performance metrics did not differ significantly between groups (Figure 1E–G), the perceptual impairments point to a sensory processing deficit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral performance metrics.

claim: Degraded ACx population-level encoding was sufficient to explain HL-associated behavioral deficits.
source: In contrast, degraded ACx population-level encoding was sufficient to explain HL-associated behavioral deficits (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the population decoder analysis.

claim: Very few ACx neurons synchronize their spike firing to very fast modulations (>100 Hz).
source: The general consensus is that very few ACx neurons synchronize their spike firing to very fast modulations (>100 Hz), and those units that encode fast rates do so with non-phase-locked responses (Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement summarizes the consensus from previous literature.

claim: Units that encode fast rates do so with non-phase-locked responses.
source: The general consensus is that very few ACx neurons synchronize their spike firing to very fast modulations (>100 Hz), and those units that encode fast rates do so with non-phase-locked responses (Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement summarizes the consensus from previous literature.

claim: Whereas auditory brainstem neurons can display a synchronized response to fast modulations, such temporal responses are transformed into a firing rate code in downstream regions, including ACx.
source: This is further supported by studies that have shown that whereas auditory brainstem neurons can display a synchronized response to fast modulations, such temporal responses are transformed into a firing rate code in downstream regions, including ACx (Palmer, 1982; Schreiner and Urbas, 1988; Frisina et al., 1990; Preuss and Müller-Preuss, 1990; Joris and Yin, 1992; Müller-Preuss et al., 1994; Rhode and Greenberg, 1994; Gaese and Ostwald, 1995; Bieser and Müller-Preuss, 1996; Krishna and Semple, 2000; Lu and Wang, 2000; Lu et al., 2001; Liang et al., 2002; Joris et al., 2004; Bendor and Wang, 2007; Wang et al., 2008; Bendor and Wang, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by extensive citations to previous research.

claim: A cortical rate code is thought to sufficiently account for AM perceptual sensitivity.
source: Thus, a cortical rate code is thought to sufficiently account for AM perceptual sensitivity (Niwa et al., 2012; 2013; 2015; von Trapp et al., 2016; Caras and Sanes, 2017) with improved sensitivity corresponding with increasing AM depth (Bieser and Müller-Preuss, 1996; Liang et al., 2002; Johnson et al., 2012; Rosen et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The current data is consistent with the literature showing minimal phase-locking and significant FR information about AM depth.
source: Our current data is consistent with this literature. Maximum phase-locking capability among our ACx units in response to AM rates of 64–512 Hz was very low, and generally not significant. In contrast, FR carried significant information about AM depth.
evidence: This is a summary of the current findings in relation to previous literature.

claim: The precise temporal structure of the population-averaged response is an important factor to representing fast AM rates.
source: Regardless of the minimal phase-locking of our ACx units to fast AM rates, our population data indicate that decoding performance increases as we decrease bin size (Figure 7B), suggesting that the precise temporal structure of the population-averaged response is an important factor to representing fast AM rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the population decoder analysis with varying bin sizes.

claim: A neural population can represent vast amounts of sensory information, but may not all be decoded during perception, leading to a discrepancy between decoding readout and behavioral performance.
source: A neural population can represent vast amounts of sensory information, but may not all be decoded during perception, which would lead to a discrepancy between the output of a decoding readout versus behavioral performance (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a general statement about neural population coding and perception.

claim: Common characteristics of the unit population may inflate the decoding readouts relative to psychophysical sensitivity.
source: Alternatively, common characteristics of the unit population may inflate the decoding readouts relative to psychophysical sensitivity.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential confounds in the decoder analysis.

claim: A linear classifier readout procedure consisting of only monotonically decreasing units outperformed one comprised of only monotonically increasing units.
source: For example, we found that a linear classifier readout procedure that consisted of only monotonically decreasing units outperformed one comprised of only monotonically increasing units (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the monotonicity analysis.

claim: If the optimal decoding of fast AM information occurs among monotonically decreasing units, this could explain the superior d' values observed for this class of neurons at lower AM depths.
source: If the optimal decoding of fast AM information occurs among monotonically decreasing units, then this could explain the superior d' values observed for this class of neurons at lower AM depths (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of monotonically decreasing units.

claim: The inclusion of all neurons more closely resembles psychometric performance.
source: That said, the inclusion of all neurons more closely resembles psychometric performance as previously suggested (Shadlen et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Population ACx activity contains sufficient sensory information to explain behavioral detection at very fast AM rates and can account for the perceptual deficits displayed by HL-reared animals.
source: Overall, our findings in awake-behaving animals indicate that population ACx activity contains sufficient sensory information to explain behavioral detection at very fast AM rates and can account for the perceptual deficits displayed by HL-reared animals.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion from the population decoder analysis.

claim: EFRs have been used to assess brainstem temporal processing across a broad range of AM rates in humans and non-human species.
source: Thus, we obtained AM depth thresholds from brainstem EFRs, which have been used to assess brainstem temporal processing across a broad range of AM rates in humans and non-human species (Boettcher et al., 2001; 2002; Leigh-Paffenroth and Fowler, 2006; Parthasarathy et al., 2010; 2014; 2016; Parthasarathy and Bartlett, 2011; 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: EFRs obtained during performance of the fast AM detection task could have been differentially modulated in Ctl and HL animals.
source: For example, Slee and David, 2015 have shown that inferior colliculus neurons are modulated by task-engagement, which leaves open the possibility that EFRs obtained during performance of the fast AM detection task could have been differentially modulated in Ctl and HL animals.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential task-engagement effects on EFRs.

claim: A subpopulation of brainstem neurons may be impaired following developmental HL, but this impairment could be masked with a population level assessment function.
source: Another possibility is that a subpopulation of brainstem neurons is impaired following developmental HL, but this impairment is masked with a population level assessment function, such as our ABRs and EFRs.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations of the EFR measurements.

claim: The findings point towards degraded neural encoding beyond the auditory brainstem as the neural origin of perceptual deficits following early auditory deprivation.
source: Regardless, our EFR measurements do not reveal a HL-related impairment that could account for behavioral deficits in fast AM rate detection. In this light, our findings point towards degraded neural encoding beyond the auditory brainstem as the neural origin of perceptual deficits following early auditory deprivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined EFR and behavioral data.

claim: Developmental conductive HL disrupts ACx synaptic and membrane properties.
source: Whole-cell recordings from ACx brain slices have revealed that developmental conductive HL disrupts ACx synaptic and membrane properties (Xu et al., 2007; Takesian et al., 2010; 2012), even for temporary manipulations (Mowery et al., 2015; 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mechanisms intrinsic to gerbil ACx could account, in part, for HL-induced behavioral deficits.
source: Therefore, it is plausible that mechanisms intrinsic to gerbil ACx could account, in part, for HL-induced behavioral deficits (Rosen et al., 2012; Buran et al., 2014a; Caras and Sanes, 2015; Ihlefeld et al., 2016; von Trapp et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ACx synaptic excitation and inhibition are normally in approximate balance.
source: Since ACx synaptic excitation and inhibition are normally in approximate balance (Tan et al., 2004; 2007; Wu et al., 2008; Tan and Wehr, 2009; Zhou et al., 2014), a net reduction of inhibition could diminish stimulus selectivity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A net reduction of inhibition could diminish stimulus selectivity (the 'iceberg effect').
source: Since ACx synaptic excitation and inhibition are normally in approximate balance (Tan et al., 2004; 2007; Wu et al., 2008; Tan and Wehr, 2009; Zhou et al., 2014), a net reduction of inhibition could diminish stimulus selectivity. This so called 'iceberg effect' implies that inhibition plays a crucial role in accurate sensory-evoked activity (Rose and Blakemore, 1974; Carandini and Ferster, 2000; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the iceberg effect concept from previous literature.

claim: The degraded synaptic inhibition observed following developmental HL may explain, in part, some of the observed behavioral impairments.
source: Thus, the degraded synaptic inhibition observed following developmental HL may explain, in part, some of the observed behavioral impairments.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the iceberg effect and previous findings of reduced inhibition.

claim: A robust correlate was found between HL-related behavioral deficits and population-level activity in ACx.
source: In fact, we found a robust correlate between HL-related behavioral deficits and population-level activity in ACx (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the population decoder analysis.

claim: The observed deficits in HL-related cortical population responses may not necessarily produce behavioral deficits since AM detection thresholds at slower modulation rates of 64 Hz were similar between Ctl versus HL animals.
source: However, our observed deficits in HL-related cortical population responses may not necessarily produce behavioral deficits since AM detection thresholds at slower modulation rates of 64 Hz were similar between Ctl versus HL animals (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the cortical population deficits.

claim: Higher levels of the auditory system may be able to remediate the deficit for slower modulation rates, but not for faster modulation rates.
source: It might be the case that higher levels of the auditory system are able to remediate the deficit for slower modulation rates, but not for faster modulation rates.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential compensatory mechanisms.

claim: The finding of superior population-level representation of task-related performance compared to individual unit metrics is consistent with previous studies from visual, somatosensory, and auditory cortices.
source: Regardless, the finding of superior population-level representation of task-related performance compared to individual unit metrics is consistent with previous studies from visual (Pouget et al., 2000; Averbeck et al., 2006; Rust and Dicarlo, 2010; Graf et al., 2011; DiCarlo et al., 2012; Pagan et al., 2013; Pagan and Rust, 2014), somatosensory (Safaai et al., 2013; Adibi et al., 2014), and auditory cortices (Middlebrooks et al., 1994; 1998; Xu et al., 1998; Miller and Recanzone, 2009; Ince et al., 2013; Pachitariu et al., 2015; Christison-Lagay et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by extensive citations to previous research.

claim: The current results provide an experimental test of population coding ideas by identifying a cortical population-level contribution to sensory deprived-related perceptual deficits.
source: The current results provide an experimental test of these ideas by identifying a cortical population-level contribution to sensory deprived-related perceptual deficits.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty and significance of the current findings.

claim: Developmental plasticity induced by abnormal changes to acoustic signals can also lead to improved sensory encoding and perception than what would have otherwise occurred.
source: Developmental plasticity induced by abnormal changes to acoustic signals can also lead to improved sensory encoding and perception than what would have otherwise occurred (Keating et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: With additional training, the animals might have eventually learned to perform the AM detection task at control levels.
source: It is possible that, with additional training, our animals would have eventually learned to perform the AM detection task at control levels.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential training effects.

claim: ACx population activity from animals reared with conductive HL were more variable across trials compared to the unit population from Ctl animals.
source: We found that ACx population activity from animals reared with conductive HL were more variable across trials compared to the unit population from Ctl animals.
evidence: This is a summary of the population-level variability analysis.

claim: The relationship between higher trial-to-trial response variability and impaired psychometric performance in HL animals is significant.
source: This signifies the relationship between higher trial-to-trial response variability and impaired psychometric performance in HL animals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the variability and behavioral data.

claim: Psychometric performance on an AM detection task benefits from lower response variability.
source: Overall, our current results support the notion that psychometric performance on an AM detection task benefits from lower response variability (von Trapp et al., 2016) since HL animals performed worse than Ctl animals and possessed less reliable cortical responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the current data and a citation to previous research.

claim: Developmental HL detrimentally increased CV of ACx population activity, possibly by reducing cortical inhibition.
source: We conclude that developmental HL detrimentally increased CV of ACx population activity (Figure 6A), possibly by reducing cortical inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion with a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The HL-induced neural encoding deficits are not observed at the brainstem, but reflect changes at higher stages in the auditory CNS network, such as ACx population activity.
source: The HL-induced neural encoding deficits are not observed at the brainstem, but reflect changes at higher stages in the auditory CNS network, such as ACx population activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion from the combined brainstem and cortical data.

claim: Bilateral conductive hearing loss was induced at postnatal day 10, just before ear canal opening.
source: For the conductive hearing loss (HL) group (n = 8, five male), bilateral conductive hearing loss was induced at postnatal day 10, just before ear canal opening as described previously (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The gerbils were reared to adulthood with a permanent bilateral conductive loss of approximately ~40 dB.
source: The gerbils were returned to their home cages for recovery and reared to adulthood with a permanent bilateral conductive loss of approximately ~40 dB (Figure 3A; Tucci et al., 1999; Buran et al., 2014a; Rosen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure with supporting citations.

claim: For normal hearing control (Ctl) animals, sound level was constant (45 or 50 dB equivalent SPL) for all AM stimuli.
source: For normal hearing control (Ctl) animals, sound level was constant (45 or 50 dB equivalent SPL) for all AM stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: For HL animals, identical stimuli were used but presented at 90 dB SPL (i.e., 45 dB louder than that used for Ctl animals), to compensate for the induced loss.
source: For HL animals, identical stimuli were used but presented at 90 dB SPL (i.e., 45 dB louder than that used for Ctl animals), to compensate for the induced loss.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.
